title: Diagnosis and SMART Objectives
text:
Do not study blindly. The first step is the Technical Diagnosis.
You must identify your bottlenecks. Are your rook endgames failing, or is it your calculation in chaotic positions?
Define SMART objectives: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound (e.g., "Increase my accuracy in pawn endgames by 15% in 3 months").
In every challenge we face in life, the first thing we always do is the diagnosis. In chess it is the same. Where do I want to get to? What steps should I take to get there? What tools do I need?
The student or chess player must have clear and realistic objectives. And then draw a temporary roadmap of what they are going to do and how they are going to achieve it.
A child who uses chess as leisure and a way to socialize with their friends is not the same as the student who wants to improve their rating and play at their maximum performance in international tournaments.
Both goals are fine, neither is better than the other, they are different, but they have different roadmaps.
An example might be a child who wants to reach a rating of 1500 by the end of the year.
Another example might be an adult who wants to learn new openings to play better in his club... but everyone should have a clear objective as to why study chess.
Take advantage right now and mark the goals you want. At the moment you lose your motivation, knowing why you decided to learn chess will help you not to quit and persist until you achieve your goals.
summary: Do not study blindly. The first step is the Technical Diagnosis.

title: The Role of the Technical Guide: Efficiency and Performance Acceleration
text:
Self-taught progression is possible, but it is intrinsically the longest path. Professional chess has evolved towards the need for a Technical Guide (Coach) that offers efficiency.
The main function of this guide is twofold:
- Objective Diagnosis: Identifying your specific knowledge gaps, which are difficult to detect through self-criticism.
- Process Acceleration: Applying proven methodologies for the effective transfer of knowledge.
It is not uncommon for professional Coaches to train with other coaches, which underscores the importance of the external perspective for the subtle analysis of the position. If you are looking for the fastest progression, prioritize structured training.
summary: Self-taught progression is possible, but it is intrinsically the longest path. Professional chess has evolved towards the need for a Technical Guide (Coach) that offers efficiency.

title: Structured Knowledge: Investment in Thesis, Not Hours. Active vs. Passive Learning
text:
Watching videos is entertainment, not training. Real learning happens under tension. Substitute passive consumption for Deliberate Practice: solve exercises without moving pieces, write down your variations, and compare them. If there is no cognitive effort, there is no neuroplasticity.
One of the most common mistakes we see is when a chess player has decided that they want to improve and "invests" thousands and thousands of hours on their own in videos and online content.
There is a lot of free content out there today, but it is generally superficial and some of it is of dubious quality.
In many cases, one studies without objectives, consumes a non-personalized syllabus (generally the one that is most readily available) and does not take into account the concepts that one must learn at that moment.
The solution is not the time invested, but the quality of the syllabus and its active application.
- Content vs. Process: Free or non-personalized material often gives you the "what" (the result of the combination) but rarely the "how" (the calculation process or strategic understanding).
- The Study Thesis: A coach or a well-designed plan provides a clear Study Thesis. Instead of consuming information at random, the student focuses on mastering a key concept (e.g., Isolated Pawn) to the point of "overdose" before moving on to the next.
- Time Savings: The real investment is not economic, but temporal. Structured content shortens the decade of self-taught study to months of measurable progress.
summary: Watching videos is entertainment, not training. Real learning happens under tension.

title: The Diagnosis Protocol and the Analytical Roadmap
text:
Your training must follow a periodization. Do not mix topics randomly. Design macrocycles (e.g., 3 months of endgames) and microcycles (e.g., 1 week of "opposite-colored bishop endgames"). Improvisation is the enemy of progress.
Serious improvement starts with formal diagnosis. It requires the experience to know not only what mistake you made, but what lack of knowledge that mistake responds to.
The diagnosis must establish a long-term Roadmap (ideally 1-2 years) and must be:
- Personalized and Scalable: The content must be neither too basic (risk of boredom) nor too advanced (risk of confusion).
- Measurable: It must include progress metrics (e.g., increase in the percentage of correct answers in 3-move tactics, or improvement in time management).
- Pattern-Based: Errors at a similar Elo level are grouped into treatable patterns. The plan must focus on eradicating these patterns.
Generally, this requires a lot of experience and self-criticism, so it is difficult to make a "self-diagnosis" yourself.
The figure of the coach is essential; they will be objective, so they will advise you better and you will know exactly what you need.
As a Coach, as soon as I know the level of the student, I know the lessons they need, at least for the next 2 years, and I have all the material prepared for it (except for the most personalized parts).
It will help you measure whether objectives are being met and rectify if they are not being achieved.
summary: Your training must follow a periodization. Do not mix topics randomly.

title: From Quantity to Density: The Effectiveness of the Session
text:
Do not count the hours, count the density of decisions. One hour solving 4 complex studies is worth more than 5 hours playing "bullet" games without thinking. Prioritize the quality and depth of analysis over volume.
Quality is always better than Quantity of study hours. This is achieved with a high density of content per session, ensuring that the syllabus is perfectly suited to the student's level.
The key is not so much the number of hours you study but the content.
We have had several cases where students reduced the number of study hours (unstructured, on their own) and achieved better results by learning specific and structured concepts that were much better suited to their level.
In the end, the mistakes made by people with a similar Elo (ranking) are identical and respond to a treatable lack of knowledge.
These mistakes are grouped into patterns, and certain key concepts can be studied to avoid repeating them (Chapter 4). Chess players with a similar rating are not so different.
It is important to know what concepts we should work on with each group of students depending on the level they have, and the progress is immediate.
If the content is too basic, the student will get bored and will not progress. If the content is too advanced, the student will not understand it and will be more confused.
Do not improvise. And as a chess player, demand a clear and concise class structure, with measurable results over time.
Organize your study. Be clear about what objective you are looking for and what concepts you need to work on. A well-designed methodology can help you improve your skills.
Remember that investing in a Coach is investing in yourself.
summary: Do not count the hours, count the density of decisions. One hour solving 4 complex studies is worth more than 5 hours playing "bullet" games without thinking.

title: The Tripartite Training System (T-T-P)
text:
I want to share with you the methodology that we apply at ChessTalentsFactory and that has given us such good results with our students. If you are a Coach, you can use it freely with your students, or if you are a player and you are studying on your own, you can adapt it to be more productive.
An effective methodology guarantees that all important aspects are covered without wasting time. The training protocol must be divided into three active phases:
- Tactics Phase (Neuronal Warm-up): Simple Pattern Exercises. Its function is twofold: to warm up the calculation capacity and motivate the student with quick solutions.
- Theoretical Phase (The Recipe): Introduction of a base concept or a specific strategic recipe per class.
- Practical Phase (Active Application): Playing games forcing the appearance of the newly learned concept (e.g., playing an opening that leads to an Isolated Pawn, if that was the topic of the class).
This immediately tests the active understanding of the concept.
Phase 1 is ideal for keeping the student always active in tactics throughout the year. In addition, it gets the brain thinking and helps the student to stay focused for the rest of the class.
The exercises don't have to be very complicated either; it also has the function of motivating the student. If in other sports there is a warm-up, why should it be different in chess? Do not start understanding concepts if your mind is not ready to calculate.
Phase 2 is the Theoretical part, which is adapted to the level of the students. In each class, the student receives one more "concept" to use in their games.
After several classes, the student already has several concepts with which to better understand the positions and devise better plans. They will not use all the concepts in the same game, but they can apply a different one in each game.
Phase 3 is the Practice of the concepts learned. Theory is useless without practice.
It is also the most playful part and where many of the students have the most fun, especially if they are children. These moments are necessary. In addition, it is especially useful in order to know if the concepts have been truly understood.
While they are playing, we point out possible improvements they could have made and remind them of the main concepts. We also practice the positions we have covered in the theoretical part.
For example, if you have worked on the concept of "Isolated Pawn," you can play an opening that leads to that pawn structure and thus have the opportunity to put that concept into practice.
We alternate opponents if possible and colors to know how to play with that structure as well as against it. In this way, the class is very complete since they perform tactics, theory and its application in practice.
Training sessions generally should last 90 minutes. This is the ideal time to not make them too heavy and for the student to be concentrated without distractions.

title: Motivation as a driving force
text:
Motivation is fluctuating; discipline is constant. Do not depend on "feeling like it." Build atomic habits: always study at the same time and in the same place to condition your brain to enter "chess mode" automatically.
Motivation is what drives us to keep going and work hard to achieve our goals. Without motivation, it is difficult to maintain the focus and discipline necessary to progress in chess and reach a highly competitive level.
Chess is complex and requires a great investment of time and effort both in studying and competing. To be competitive, we need to study regularly and be active.
However, the routine of study and practice can seem boring and monotonous at some point, which can lead to demotivation.
Motivation is what drives us to keep going, even when things get tough. When we are motivated, we are willing to invest time and effort in our training, and to keep going despite the obstacles we may encounter.
We can also maintain a positive attitude and focus on progress rather than immediate results. Without motivation, it is difficult to maintain the commitment necessary to reach our goals.
In certain cases, it depends on the moment in which one finds oneself. For example, you don't have the same motivation to study chess after playing three very good tournaments as you do after three very bad ones.
Even outside of chess, extraordinary events in our daily life will affect our mood and our rhythm of life.
In many tournaments, we see poor performances due to lack of motivation, and it is a problem at all levels.
How to deal with motivation? I will focus on the most common cases.
summary: Motivation is fluctuating; discipline is constant. Do not depend on "feeling like it." Build atomic habits: always study at the same time and in the same place to condition your brain to enter "chess mode" automatically.

title: Infant Cognitive Development
text:
In formative stages (U-10, U-12), the goal is not the Elo, it is the acquisition of patterns. The child's brain is a sponge for tactics. Prioritize serious fun and solving geometric problems over dense opening theory.
Sometimes children are discovering a new sport, they are experimenting. There are children who clearly like it and others who do not. However, many need to understand it better and need more time to become seriously interested.
This is a normal process. Parents, teachers, and coaches should be very patient and promote chess as an entertaining game, especially at an early age.
If we are able to convey to them the passion for chess, even if it is not at a competitive level, later on it is easy for them to become interested in it by themselves. This would be the natural learning process.
That is why in the first classes it is very important to connect with the student, invest time in getting to know their hobbies, their daily life, and create a calm environment where learning chess is fun.
There are great teachers who, in spite of not having reached a great competitive level as players, have been excellent coaches conveying that passion for chess to children at a very early age.
FIDE (International Chess Federation) itself has several official titles as Trainer depending on the level of specialization and its function.
One of the common problems is inducing the child to learn competitive chess or more technical classes when such interest has not been awakened in him/her yet.
It is important not to rush in these cases, to give them the freedom to simply play and not to worry about the level they can reach.
An excessive pressure to compete or force them to study formally when they do not really feel like it generates the opposite effect, and in many cases, they end up leaving chess even though they have great potential.
Sometimes parents, with the best intentions and with the idea of supporting their children, can create additional pressure on them.
summary: In formative stages (U-10, U-12), the goal is not the Elo, it is the acquisition of patterns. The child's brain is a sponge for tactics.

title: Frustration Management
text:
Chess is a zero-sum game where losing hurts. Teach (and learn) to separate your personal worth from your sports result. Defeat is simply a "data point" that points to a technical error to correct, not a character flaw.
Solution: At the Academy, we have found that group classes can work very well for those students who do not yet have an intense interest in chess because they can socialize and play with other students of the same level. Sometimes they win and sometimes they lose, avoiding frustrations while learning the values of the sport.
Later, when their interest in chess grows, it can be considered that they participate in individual, smaller, or more technical classes.
You can also look for what motivates the child most in the world of chess (for example, tactics) and strengthen that part while teaching the virtues of other aspects of the game.
In these cases, you can also include alternative exercises related to chess to encourage their curiosity or playful activities to connect with them.
It is also important to know their references or show them inspiring examples so that they can forge their own goals.
summary: Chess is a zero-sum game where losing hurts. Teach (and learn) to separate your personal worth from your sports result.

title: Motivation in Underachieving Adults. Neuroplasticity
text:
From the age of 40 onwards, pure calculation speed may decrease, but schematic (crystallized) understanding can continue to increase. Compensate for slower speed with better prophylaxis and a more solid positional repertoire.
Children are faster learners in general, and chess is no different.
The mind at that age (especially 5-16 years old) absorbs and processes knowledge very fast. They also have more free time and fewer worries.
From 5 to 16 years old is the best age to learn chess and to invest our resources in its learning.
Until the age of 40, the chess player can reach their best performance, and in fact, the vast majority of current top 100 chess players are young people under 30 years old.
With technology and the rise of online chess, the experience that used to be acquired after many years of study and practice can now be acquired in months or even weeks from your own home.
Another important factor is that in today's information age, knowledge is becoming more accessible to new generations every year, it is of better quality, and you can reach a higher level faster than previous generations.
Although, of course, there are always exceptions and there are great players who even in adulthood (over 40 years old) have not only maintained their level but have improved it. Viswanathan Anand is a clear example.
The effort behind this is incalculable, but they are a reference to follow for all of us.
From the age of 40 onwards, our mind progressively enters a decline, it works slower, reflexes are lost, and we will not get the same results if we keep doing the same. And it gets worse from the age of 50 onwards.
If as time goes by our mind gradually loses performance and new generations can reach our level of knowledge faster, it is easy to understand why many adults lower their level drastically, in many cases without playing badly, but it is the natural process.
But don't worry! Like everything in life, there is a solution. Once we understand how the mind works over the years, we can anticipate this situation.
If your performance has dropped a lot after the age of 40, the first thing to do is to accept it. And it is reversible! Generally, it usually happens because your dedication to chess has fallen a little, sometimes without you realizing it and in many cases because of the stress of work, which added to the above explained makes the perfect conditions to gradually lower our performance.
summary: From the age of 40 onwards, pure calculation speed may decrease, but schematic (crystallized) understanding can continue to increase. Compensate for slower speed with better prophylaxis and a more solid positional repertoire.

title: Reversal of a bad trend in adults
text:
If you cannot train to improve, train to maintain. Solve 5 daily tactics problems to keep neuronal connections active. Inactivity is corrosive; minimum maintenance prevents technical atrophy.
The solution involves the accompaniment of a coach and a greater investment of time in chess.
If as a child, youngster, or early adult we studied chess to improve our level, from the age of 40 we should train at least to acquire new knowledge and compensate for the passage of time and the rise of new generations in order not to lose our level.
Training after this age may not mean an improvement in ranking, perhaps only a maintenance of level over time. But what is confirmed is that not training means, according to statistics, a loss of level in most cases.
At the Academy, we focus on children, but we also work with several adults and many of them not only manage to maintain their fitness over time, but also improve their rating and get better results.
At this age, it is very important to work on tactics regularly to improve reflexes and confidence.
Time pressure is also a common problem, although in many cases it is due to inactivity and lack of competition.
Also, game analysis is especially useful for this type of profile as they usually have a consolidated opening repertoire.
I wanted to give an honest account of what happens to a chess player with the passage of time. I have seen and worked with several students who were in this situation.
It may seem discouraging; however, those who have taken action, decided to seek advice, and invested time in learning have made significant progress and even reversed their situation by recovering their rating and improving it.
The main problem occurs when no action is taken in time and no action is planned. At this age, work and family life take up a lot of time, but competition is unforgiving.
For many adults or retired chess players, chess becomes a hobby and they neglect their level. But if you want to compete and become your best version even after 40 years old, with effort and dedication if you really want it, you will not have any problem.
Do you have the same objectives as before? What does competitive chess mean to you now? And in 10 years? Do you have a plan to invest more time as you get older?
summary: If you cannot train to improve, train to maintain. Solve 5 daily tactics problems to keep neuronal connections active.

title: Motivation after poor results in tournaments. Competitive Resilience
text:
After a bad streak, do not look for immediate results. Return to the fundamentals. Play solid, regain confidence with known schemes, and avoid unnecessary complications until you recover your mental "form."
It is natural to feel demotivated after a series of bad and discouraging tournaments. There are several ways to motivate yourself to continue studying chess:
- Reflect on mistakes: Instead of feeling discouraged, we use our mistakes to learn and improve. We analyze our games to identify mistakes and reflect on what we could have done differently. We should use these mistakes to create a study plan to work on our weaknesses.
- Set realistic goals: We will define realistic goals for our training and set a plan of action to achieve them. This will give us purpose in our study.
- Vary the study routine: If we are studying chess the same way over and over again, it can become monotonous. We can try varying our study routine, including different types of exercises and learning strategies to maintain motivation.
- Talk to our Coach: We can talk to our coach about our feelings and frustrations. Coaches give advice and guidance to help analyze what is going on and how to correct it.
- Inspiration: We should look for inspiration from other chess players, either professional players or friends who have gone through the same problems. It can also appear in books, articles, videos...
- Take a break: If we are overwhelmed or exhausted, we may need to take a break from chess competition and study. It's okay!
We can take some time to do other things we enjoy and come back to chess when we feel better, more confident, and more motivated. Sometimes stopping for a while is good and we see everything in a better perspective.
To motivate ourselves to study chess after a series of bad tournaments it is important to reflect on our mistakes, set realistic goals, vary our study routine, talk to our coach, look for inspiration and, if necessary, take a break.
With perseverance and a positive attitude, we can overcome those bumps and continue to progress smoothly.
summary: After a bad streak, do not look for immediate results. Return to the fundamentals.

title: Motivation after extra-sporting situations (Set & Setting)
text:
Eliminate distractions. "Deep Work" requires isolation. If you have extra-sporting problems, use chess as a refuge of logical order, not as an extra source of stress.
It is understandable that extra-sporting events or situations can affect our motivation. In many cases, studies, work, or family life can influence our daily routine.
Remember why you started studying chess and what goals you had set for yourself. If you focus on the results you want to achieve, you can regain the motivation you need to keep going.
Relive what excited you. Watch chess games of world top players, read chess books, attend tournaments...
Set small goals: It is always easier if we set small goals. For example, dedicate an hour a day to study an opening or practice chess tactics. Small good habits maintained for a long time generate big transformations.
Work on your mindset: Working on our mindset can help us maintain a positive attitude.
summary: Eliminate distractions. "Deep Work" requires isolation.

title: Motivations and benefits of playing chess. Transfer of Skills
text:
Chess trains Decision Making under Uncertainty. The skills you develop (time management, risk calculation, objectivity) are transferable to professional and personal life. Value chess for this mental gymnastics.
Fun and entertainment: Chess is an entertaining sport with which we can share an activity with our friends. Learning chess can help us enjoy the game even more, understand the positions better, and optimize our results.
Promotes socialization: It can be played in a team or against another person and promotes socialization among players.
Improves memory: In chess, you must remember previous positions and moves. Studying chess develops memory and improves the ability to remember information. Lately, it is one of the most demanded activities by parents in their children's education.
Cognitive development: It requires a high level of concentration, memory, and cognitive skills. Learning chess will help us to develop and improve these skills.
Fosters patience and perseverance: In chess, patience and perseverance are required to improve and succeed. These qualities can be transferred to other areas of life.
Improves problem-solving skills: Chess is a strategy sport that requires us players to think about our moves and our opponent's moves. Chess stimulates problem-solving and decision-making skills.
Increases creativity: It fosters creativity and imagination, especially when playing in situations where there is no single correct variant.
Learning to plan: Develops planning and organizational skills (plans and strategies).
Increases self-esteem: At a competitive level, it is possible to obtain important sporting achievements that allow us to increase our self-esteem and confidence.
You enjoy a healthier life: Chess has proven to be beneficial to avoid some mental illnesses and improve our mental health in general.
Studies have shown that playing chess regularly can help prevent dementia and Alzheimer's disease, as it requires a large amount of brain activity and can help keep memory and thinking sharp.
Also, playing chess can be a therapeutic and relaxing activity that can help reduce anxiety and depression.
Remember that motivation is something that fluctuates over time, and sometimes it is normal to experience periods of disinterest.
The important thing is not to get discouraged and look for ways to regain the motivation to move forward with our goals.
Whatever your case is, chess is very beneficial for all ages, so I encourage you to keep training and always look for your best version.

title: Tactics as a warm-up
text:
In our experience, at the Academy we always start chess classes with tactics, at least the first few minutes. It is part of the methodology.
Since the implementation of this step, we have seen how our students achieved better results and progressed faster.
There are 2 main reasons: The first one, as we have mentioned in the methodology part, is that doing tactics exercises helps to activate the brain and helps the students to be more concentrated for the theoretical part.
In fact, it is normal that, even with simple exercises, it is difficult for them to solve the first ones because the brain is not yet activated to think.
The second reason is one of control. We make sure that all students practice tactics regularly. In the end, if we are able to solve for example just 20 exercises per week, at the end of the year we will be solving more than 1000 tactical exercises which will help us to progress a lot.
And although we all know the benefits of practicing tactics, not everyone has the time or the will to do it independently and regularly.
The same happens with physical activity; how many times have we refused to go to the gym or go for a run due to lack of will? However, it is easier if you have someone to motivate you and help you.
Now that we understand tactics and calculation in depth and understand their importance... how do they affect our performance and what can we do?
Tactics are always important because a serious tactical mistake can cause you to lose all the advantage accumulated in a game.
Having remarked this, tactics are especially important in players who are just starting out, as they allow them to generate great advantages through simple calculations. Many of them ignore these threats. They do not have enough preparation to anticipate 1, 2, or 3 moves.
summary: In our experience, at the Academy we always start chess classes with tactics, at least the first few minutes. It is part of the methodology.

title: Study and assimilation of tactical patterns
text:
There are also tactical patterns (pin, double attack, deflection...) that are often repeated and can appear several times in the same game.
If we train these patterns, it will be easy for us to recognize them and apply them in our favor to avoid threats or generate an advantage in our games.
As the level of the players rises, these simple calculations are easily avoided by both players, and although even grandmasters can make serious tactical mistakes, it is normal that this does not happen and the strategic and theoretical knowledge are more decisive.
How can I improve tactics depending on my level?
If you are a player who is starting in the world of chess, you should invest a large part of your study in the realization of Tactics. I recommend that you work on patterns from very basic tactics (1 or 2 moves) and gradually increase the difficulty until you master the subject completely.
Once you have mastered a tactical pattern you can change to another pattern and you will acquire new "references" that will help you to detect possible tactics in your games.
The good thing is that you will notice the results immediately as it influences a lot in beginner level games.
summary: There are also tactical patterns (pin, double attack, deflection...) that are often repeated and can appear several times in the same game. If we train these patterns, it will be easy for us to recognize them and apply them in our favor to avoid threats or generate an advantage in our games.

title: Tactics at intermediate and advanced levels
text:
Some of the techniques we apply are:
- Alternate exercises with different patterns. In a real game you will not know if there is a viable option to combine or not, only your instinct will know how to appreciate the various tactical reasons that can make us think that there is a combination. Intuition must be promoted.
When we are practicing tactics, we already know that there is some calculation solution in the position. One of the ways to raise the level is to practice random exercises that do not always follow the same pattern.
- Combine basic exercise routines with very complex exercises. A very interesting study practice is to use the time you have allocated for tactics, for example, a 15-minute session, to solve the maximum number of basic exercises. These can be exercises of 1 or 2 moves. An example would be to have solved 18 exercises in that time, 15 minutes.
Another day, you can use those 15 minutes to solve only one very complex exercise of 6 or 7 moves, with several variations.
In the first case we are working on tactics to acquire mental agility and basic patterns (having more references).
In the second case we are working on depth, visualization, and even complex calculation.
Both are necessary and will help us to calculate better and more efficiently in chess.
For an advanced level, most of these patterns are already known and it is more interesting to work on calculation.
The reason is that in calculation there are more variables and therefore the complexity increases and gets even closer to a real game situation.
In calculation we analyze moves not only to win material or give mate, but it can also be to obtain a positional advantage.
The assessment of the position after analyzing several variations weighs more than in tactics because they are not always winning lines.
They can be analyses where they end in equality or slight advantage and to value these positions in the mind anticipating the moves is more complex.
summary: Some of the techniques we apply are: - Alternate exercises with different patterns. In a real game you will not know if there is a viable option to combine or not, only your instinct will know how to appreciate the various tactical reasons that can make us think that there is a combination.

title: Tactics in inactive players
text:
Tactics is also one of the frequent problems in players who have been inactive for a long time. Even in high-level inactive players. The reason for this is the lack of tension, as they are not used to thinking under time pressure as they used to.
It is very important to do problems and practice Blitz games (3+2) after long periods of inactivity.
The practice of problems will force the brain to get back to the level required to think correctly and the Blitz games will help to gain confidence and to dare to play fast in complicated positions.
Why do we recommend 3+2 Blitz games (3 minutes and 2 seconds increment per move) in these cases?
Because in long periods of inactivity the brain tends to become blocked under time pressure. The 3+2 rhythm is the ideal test to "stress" our mind again, but giving enough time to be able to choose good moves in a short period of time. In addition, it allows for quick and easy calculations.
Shorter rhythms would make us directly unable to think because we have to make very quick decisions and, in many cases, it becomes a race against the clock rather than a game of chess. Chance becomes more important.
Slower rhythms would not generate enough stress to force us to make immediate decisions or at least not in all the games played.
summary: Tactics is also one of the frequent problems in players who have been inactive for a long time. Even in high-level inactive players.

title: Calculation in advanced players
text:
If we remarked the importance of tactics in the most basic levels, calculation can be the great differentiator as we progress.
The difference between calculation and tactics lies in 2 factors: depth and the evaluation of positions.
If tactics can be encompassed through patterns or forced themes with which to achieve advantage (they’ll always be easy evaluations since one side achieves a great advantage), calculation requires analysis of several variations (depth), evaluation of these, and subsequent comparison.
While calculating, in order to evaluate a variant correctly, the final position must not contain tactical patterns because they can hinder its evaluation.
Therefore, in some cases, we will need to calculate a large number of moves to have a clear view of what we are thinking and to be able to assign an accurate evaluation.
Depth is the number of moves and variations calculated.
The more variations and the more moves we calculate correctly, the more accurate our evaluation will be, but at the same time the more time we will need to think and the more complex it will be.
Evaluation consists of assigning a valuation to each calculated line and choosing the one with the best valuation for us.
The more moves we calculate, the more difficult it will be to visualize the final position and therefore its evaluation.
summary: If we remarked the importance of tactics in the most basic levels, calculation can be the great differentiator as we progress. The difference between calculation and tactics lies in 2 factors: depth and the evaluation of positions.

title: Depth vs. Evaluation
text:
A totally false and very common myth for those who do not know chess in depth is to believe that grandmasters calculate many more moves than their opponents and that this is the main difference with a less experienced player.
That is, that the key is that they analyze more deeply than their opponents and that is not exactly so.
What really happens is that they discard many bad variations more easily and evaluate more accurately the final positions they calculate.
Although they can also calculate more deeply, it is not the main difference.

title: Creativity and Tactics
text:
As a curiosity, there is a type of problems that are artistic compositions called "chess studies" that generally have a tactical and calculation component.
They do not have to be real positions; a problem is posed with an atypical solution that challenges the natural reasoning of thinking in chess.
The studies work very well to work on creativity. These types of exercises are used at a high level and at the Academy we also practice them from time to time to encourage new ways of thinking.
Another interesting and innovative way to practice creativity is "blind calculation". This involves solving a problem without seeing the pieces on the board. You can also memorize a position, hide your pieces, and ask for their location.
MIDDLEGAMES AND ENDGAMES
There are a number of "basic concepts” that every good chess player should possess.
The classical players began to illustrate these concepts.
Even so, I find it incredible that despite the technology and the great theoretical advances in chess, there is no emphasis on what concepts should be studied according to the level or rating and how to approach them.
Yes, there are a lot of publications that explain individual topics (and some are very good) but it is difficult to find publications that detail a list of recommended concepts according to one's level.
In Square 65 we address this issue.
On several occasions students with a basic level asked me for recommendations about the openings they had studied but my answer has always been the same:
"If you want to progress quickly you need to acquire middlegame and endgame concepts to be able to design good plans regardless of the opening you play".
Acquiring these concepts properly takes months and even years of study so choose well where and how you invest your study time. As a reference, at the Academy we do not work on the opening repertoire until at least the student reaches around 1600 rating (over the board).

title: List of concepts to study according to level
text:
A mistake because of which many beginners do not progress is that they invest many hours of their study in openings (instead of Middlegame and Endgame).
Surely the fact that you study a series of moves that you know for sure you are going to repeat in many of your games may make you think that this is the most important thing to study, but the opposite is true.
And you may think that you will never play an endgame or a middlegame like the ones you are studying, and it may even be so, but the knowledge you acquire helps you to understand those positions and also many similar positions (these will be given to you in games). We refer to the transversal knowledge.
When you study a thematic plan or a pawn structure you don't need to play that specific position to take advantage of it. Just the fact of having more references will help you to compare, evaluate and play better in general.
Besides, most games are decided in the Middlegame and Endgame. Unless the opponent makes a serious mistake, you will hardly win in the Opening.
Every chess player has a limited number of hours per year to study. It can be 50 or it can be 500. Invest those hours appropriately.
If in each study session you acquire one more reference of a concept, a pawn structure, a strategic idea, an endgame... at the end of all the sessions of the year you will have a huge internalized list that will give you a global vision to design better plans and make better games.
I am going to provide you with a list of basic concepts that every chess player should master very well in order to reach an intermediate level (1500-1800 rating).
Both a basic and an intermediate level require the study of many concepts, but mainly Middlegame and Endgame.
And yes, in these lists I also include opening concepts, but I am not referring to theoretical knowledge, but rather conceptual.
This is my reference and it would have been very useful for me to know this list years ago in my training to identify where to prioritize my learning.
A list of key concepts that should be studied for a basic level are:
Openings: Center, initiative, development, dynamics, strong and weak squares....
Middlegame: The rule of 2 weaknesses, the Zugzwang, the king's safety, not moving the same piece twice, good bishop vs bad knight, good knight vs bad bishop, bishop pair vs knight pair, domination, fortress, stalemate, the chess classics....
Endgames: Basic pawn endgames, advanced pawn endgames, the opposition, triangulation, the square rule, basic mates (queen, rook...), basic rook endgames, classical endgames...
A list of key concepts that should be studied for an intermediate level are:
Openings: First schemes, basic repertoire, simple openings and typical reactions to possible gambits, typical opening mistakes...
Middlegame: Doubled pawns, dynamics in chess, direct attack on the king, patience, schematic thinking, Grunfeld pawn structure, isolated pawn (how to play with it and against it), passed pawns, hanging pawns, Stonewal

title: Non-acceptance of defeat and subsequent consequences of defeat in children
text:
This is an mistake that occurs at all levels. Chess is a mental sport where one player thinks more accurately than another and it is not always easy to assimilate.
At a very basic level in children who are just starting it is a normal process.
It is essential to make them see that defeat is part of the game and one does not always win. It is especially important to educate children correctly in the first championships they play, encouraging competitive intensity but always based on values.
The first competitions generate an adrenaline and pressure that children are not used to.
It is normal for children to feel frustrated and disappointed when they lose a game of chess or any other game in which they have invested time and effort.
However, there are some strategies we can use to help children manage their emotions and deal with defeat in a healthy way:
Teach them the importance of having fun with chess. We must make sure that children understand that the important thing is not to win or lose, but to enjoy the game itself. This can help reduce the pressure and stress they may feel when playing.
Let him/her know that defeat is part of the process. We must explain that in any game or sport there are winners and losers, and that losing is a natural part of the learning process.
Encourage them to keep practicing and improving their skills, regardless of the outcome of each game.
Connect with their emotions. If children feel frustrated or sad after losing a game, we should listen to their feelings and encourage them to express themselves.
They should know that it is normal to feel this way and that it is okay to cry or vent from time to time.
Reinforce the value of effort and perseverance: We have to make sure that they understand that effort and perseverance are more important than the final result.
Congratulate them on their achievements and on the hard work they have put into their games, regardless of the outcome.
Teach losing with sportsmanship. It is normal to congratulate the winner and accept defeat with grace and sportsmanship. This not only helps their personal growth, but also fosters healthier and more positive relationships with other players.
summary: This is an mistake that occurs at all levels. Chess is a mental sport where one player thinks more accurately than another and it is not always easy to assimilate.

title: Non-acceptance of defeat and subsequent consequences of defeat in adults
text:
This mistake is frequent in children, but at another level also in adults and masters! There are several players whose sporting performance decreases a lot because they are not able to forget a defeat.
It is because they have invested many hours studying, they are able to get advantageous positions and play with mastery, but at a given moment a serious mistake can make them lose a game incomprehensibly.
It happens at all levels.
If we are not able to recover from this emotional blow quickly during a tournament and we go on to play the next round thinking about the previous game, it is easy to be conditioned to make bad moves and lose again, aggravating the problem even more.
There are tournaments where 2 or even 3 rounds are played on the same day.
The time to recover is minimal and the opponent that you may play against after the defeat can be as hard as or harder than the previous one.
In this case we must be aware that we must continue competing and the defeat cannot condition us to play badly in the next rounds.
summary: This mistake is frequent in children, but at another level also in adults and masters! There are several players whose sporting performance decreases a lot because they are not able to forget a defeat.

title: Recovering from defeats
text:
The best solution is to understand the mistake made and then forget about the game during the tournament. You can use engines (computer analysis) to find out which move you should have made.
Once you understand the decisive mistake, it is easier to assimilate it, forget it and "forgive" yourself. Remember that we will always have more games to play better.
You should also not forget that the opponents make serious mistakes in positions where we were lost. Today it may be our turn and another day we may be the lucky ones to win a lost game.
Once the tournament is over, you should analyze your games thoroughly so as not to make the same mistakes again.
In this way, if you are able to recover quickly from defeats, you will be able to take advantage of them and be more regular.
summary: The best solution is to understand the mistake made and then forget about the game during the tournament. You can use engines (computer analysis) to find out which move you should have made.

title: Lack of ductility when being trained
text:
This is a common mistake, especially at intermediate levels. If you decide to train with a coach, it’s the coach who is in charge of defining which concepts to work on.
In the same way that when you go to the doctor for a serious problem, they are the ones who diagnose you, right? In chess it is the same.
But some students choose to "self-diagnose". You can share your opinions of course, but if you put yourself in the hands of a professional, they should be the one to make the decisions about what issues to address. The Coach has a specific methodology.
If as a student you demand a solution or a specific subject you run the risk of it not adapting to your style or the level you need. Demand a roadmap, but not specific classes to your liking.
If you propose the theme yourself, you do not give the coach the option of a second professional opinion, so that the coach can assess what you really need. And if you do not progress, you will not know if it is the fault of a poor transmission of knowledge from the coach or an inadequate choice of the subject matter on your part.
The expert is the coach and if the solutions they propose are not effective or you do not feel comfortable with them you can always change Coach. Trust them and be positive.
summary: This is a common mistake, especially at intermediate levels. If you decide to train with a coach, it’s the coach who is in charge of defining which concepts to work on.

title: Lack of patience during the study of chess
text:
A problem that I have also seen in certain occasions is abandoning the study of chess because the desired results were not achieved. Sometimes even within 1 or 2 months.
Learning chess requires time and therefore patience. If extraordinary results could be achieved in 1 month, everyone would be a master. If you have high goals, be consistent and give yourself large margins of time to achieve them. Besides, the type of chess player you are and the way you have been trained up to your current moment also influence at that.
Depending on the profile of the students, there are students who have a similar level in tactics, openings, middlegame, endgame, strategy... and others who are really brilliant in some of these areas and show quite a lot of weaknesses in others. What happens with this?
It is neither good nor bad, they are different profiles. There are students who have worked on tactics intensively for years reaching a very high level and yet they have a much lower level because strategically they are below average. Others do not stand out in any particular area but do not have clear weaknesses either.
Therefore, there are 2 types of students: some who gradually improve their ranking little by little because they are very balanced in all areas and their improvement is continuous and proportional and other students who are more irregular, stand out in a specific area, but are weak in others.
The latter need several months of work to train the parts where they have more weaknesses. Once these weaknesses have been worked on, the results allow them to increase their ranking in an accelerated manner, which is why they are experiencing occasional, but large-scale improvements.
In both scenarios the level of progress may be the same only that one student may have made gradual monthly progress while another student may experience large increases in 2 specific months reaching the same ranking as the first one.
In this second profile where learning has been more irregular, perseverance is even more important. Leaving learning in the middle can deprive us of our final objective.
If you are thinking of abandoning the study of chess, also consider whether the material you are studying is advisable, if your study methodology is correct, if you are being adequately advised, if you are using quality sources, if you are investing the necessary time...
In the previous chapters we have already shared a series of tips that you should apply to optimize your study. If you are not applying them strictly, it will take you longer to achieve your results.
summary: A problem that I have also seen in certain occasions is abandoning the study of chess because the desired results were not achieved. Sometimes even within 1 or 2 months.

title: Lack of ambition, fear of defeat and fanaticism for draws
text:
Surely in some tournament you have seen a player who has made a high number of draws. We refer to a percentage equal to or higher than 40% (of course discarding games of world tops with a rating higher than 2600).
This type of results is linked to insecurity. It is a big problem because, psychologically, the fact that we are getting many draws usually leads to games that should be won ending up as draws, while the number of defeats remains constant.
I must admit that this is without a doubt one of the psychological problems that I have dealt with the most as a coach, it occurs quite frequently and we have worked on it with many of our students. We all have insecurities at some point, but it is especially common in students of 1800-2000 rating.
It is also easily reversible, although it must be detected as early as possible.
Especially in this rating bracket (1800-2000) is where the student has already acquired a strong knowledge base, is progressing at an intermediate level and is going to make the jump to an advanced level.
It also coincides with the beginning of the preparation of a professional opening repertoire where basic tactics no longer serve to improve our score.
To keep progressing, we must win against tough opponents who are not going to lose tactically, many of the games will be decided in details and especially in endgames.
At this level we usually come out of the opening equal and it is not easy to unbalance in the middlegame.
A common mistake is to accept or offer a draw when we see that the opponent does not make any clear tactical mistake that could give us an advantage.
What is the problem with this? When making quick draws, (generally in less than 40 moves and without a struggle) the game played has no interest for analysis since most likely there have been no big mistakes and no time pressure.
Both didactically and in terms of improving the ranking score, it is practically as if it had not been played. It is not useful and nothing is learned.
If you get into the habit of doing this repeatedly, what is the point of going to the trouble of training hard and traveling to tournaments to get nothing useful out of it?
What is worse, this kind of behavior generates a lack of confidence and makes us look for draw positions without realizing it.
The games must be played and we must try to give 100%. If this behavior is detected, it must be eradicated as soon as possible because as long as the student continues to act in this way, they will be limited and will not be able to progress to the next level.
summary: Surely in some tournament you have seen a player who has made a high number of draws. We refer to a percentage equal to or higher than 40% (of course discarding games of world tops with a rating higher than 2600).

title: The fight to the end of the game
text:
The solution is simple. The first thing to do is to analyze the games and make the student understand that in drawn games without a fight nothing is learned and there is no sense in studying chess for that purpose.
Once the student understands this, the second step is to get them to commit themselves and the coach to try for at least 6 months or 1 year not to offer or accept draw under any circumstances. Also, not to repeat the position 3 times intentionally.
Of course, some games may end in a draw like king vs king or similar.
This practice is another technique used in our High Performance Academy with incredible results in a great number of students.
This simple gesture will reduce the number of draws drastically. The draws that are produced will be fought, in very long games where they will be very interesting to analyze in the classes to later work on the technique of those endgames.
The students are more concentrated.
In equal positions they are not thinking about offering draws because this option does not exist. They first look for all options to win and therefore get better results.
Games that ended in a draw become victory due to mistakes of the rivals because of exhaustion and, as a last option and in a lower percentage end in a draw.
They also save time because they don't have to spend a second thinking about whether or not to accept the draw offer. They are directly rejected and concentrate on looking for the best move of the position.
A technique used by some clever players in a slightly inferior position is to offer a draw when they are in time trouble. In some chess players it generates indecision and they end up accepting the offer because they have spent a lot of time thinking about whether to accept the draw offer or not instead of thinking about the position.
Once the student is committed to giving their best and seeking victory in every game, they usually have immediate positive results.
The subsequent follow-up during the following months is also a fundamental part. It is key to reinforce this behavior and this way of competing in order not to lose this value.
In this process we move from having a psychological blockage to gaining the value and recognition of struggle and perseverance.

For example, some players prefer dynamic and tactical openings, while others prefer more positional and solid openings.
It is also common to "prepare", that is, to study the openings that our opponents use frequently in order to know which the best options to face them are.

title: Introduction to the Openings. Classic games
text:
We have practiced a lot of tactics; we know the basic patterns and we have mastered certain middlegame and endgame concepts.
How do we approach the study of openings in order to start competing?
It is very important to learn the concepts of Development, Center and Initiative.
Although they are seen at an early level they can be trained with a very high degree of complexity since even strong players have shown in some games, weaknesses generated by the misapplication of these concepts in Openings.
Classic games are often very instructive to exemplify the problems we may have when making mistakes in the opening.
By classic games we refer to games that were played many decades ago where a master applies these basic concepts correctly and the corrective plan is clearly understood.
It is necessary to put them in context, there were no engines and the information was not transmitted as it is now and therefore there were a greater number of mistakes and more serious mistakes.
This may seem to detract from the games, but, on the contrary, we can use it to understand the typical mistakes when playing badly as our opponents also make similar mistakes!
If you master tactics, acquire the basic concepts properly and apply the most elementary concepts of openings, you can easily reach an intermediate and even advanced level.
How do we study openings from an intermediate level (1600 rating)? And for an advanced one?

title: Theoretical Opening Study for intermediate level players
text:
As you acquire concepts, you improve and reach a level where you have to start studying openings in a theoretical way seriously. The first thing you should know is what openings or what kind of variations to learn.
If you are entering an intermediate level and you are going to start studying your first openings, I recommend that you choose openings that are easy to learn and by this, I mean openings that do not involve many hours of study or an advanced understanding of typical positions. Do not start with complex openings.
For example, a bad choice would be a Sicilian-Dragon Defense as the first opening to study, since the theory of this variant has advanced a lot, it is very complex and requires many hours of study to understand it well.
In addition, you would have to understand very advanced concepts of strategy that occur frequently in the middlegame such as quality positional sacrifices.
However, it is an ideal opening for a high level to complete their understanding of advanced concepts of strategy and as an option to search for complex positions against difficult opponents.
What openings would we recommend for an intermediate level?
Those that are easy to study, require little understanding and few hours of study. The Slav, the Four Knights or the Italian fit very well into this description, as they are symmetrical openings in many variations and there are many playable plans for both.
Also, of interest could be those that can be played schematically and in a very similar way, regardless of the opponent's game. In this sector we could include the English, the Reti or the London System.
The advantage of a scheme is that you can learn it in 3 lessons with your coach and use the rest of the time to continue progressing in Middlegame and Endgames.
Remember that Middlegame strategy and Endgame technique is what will make you progress to the next level. The more time you spend on it and less on Openings, the faster you will improve your rating.
summary: As you acquire concepts, you improve and reach a level where you have to start studying openings in a theoretical way seriously. The first thing you should know is what openings or what kind of variations to learn.

title: Benefits of studying certain openings
text:
An interesting way to approach the study of openings at an intermediate level is to think about the benefits that such an opening brings to subsequent learning in the long term.
For example, one of the openings we like to teach is the Berlin versus the Spanish. The reason is that the main line leads to an endgame after the first few moves and the Spanish is the opening most often used by White.
This will force us statistically to play many endgames and after the subsequent analysis of the games it will be very useful for us to improve in them.
Beyond the fact that the Berlin Defense may be more or less interesting or you may like it more or less, we can use it to gain experience in endgames and strengthen ourselves in this area.
We will be studying Openings and Endgames at the same time!
You don't have to play it all your life, you can use it for 6 months or 1 year intensively until you notice your improvement in endgames.
When I was young, I applied this technique and it helped me a lot to play more finals and therefore understand them better. The long-term result is very positive and now we apply it at the Academy.
summary: An interesting way to approach the study of openings at an intermediate level is to think about the benefits that such an opening brings to subsequent learning in the long term. For example, one of the openings we like to teach is the Berlin versus the Spanish.

title: Theoretical Opening Study for advanced level players
text:
Generally, when you have properly learned 1 opening/defense against the main openings of both White and Black and mastered the key concepts that every good chess player should know (see chapter 4), congratulations! you are entering the Advanced level, generally we are talking about players of 1700-1800 rating and above. At this level there are several key points.
To reach International Master (IM) level you should have a minimum knowledge of most of the openings and the most classical middlegames.
It is highly recommended that you expand your opening repertoire and study several openings.
The reason is simply that you will play different middlegames and endgames. This will give you experience in new positions and will serve you to have more references and to be able to compare those positions with others you have played previously.
You don't play the same middlegames and endgames if you play one opening or another. In the long run, you will be more experienced, more versatile and it will even help you to have better results if in the future you go back to playing your old repertoire because your general knowledge and understanding will be much better. Transversal Learning.
If in the intermediate level I advised you not to study complex openings and even recommended you to play with schemes, for this level it’s the opposite.
You will have to keep improving in middlegame and endgame, but what will help you to keep growing and make the jump to the next level is the knowledge of openings.
And by knowledge of openings, I do not refer only and exclusively to the memorization of moves, which does not help much, but to the understanding and connection with the middlegame.
At this level it is necessary to invest many hours of study in the understanding of typical plans, theory, novelties...
And since you are going to do it, the greater the complexity of playing well for the opponent in case of not knowing the opening, the more options you will have to take advantage.
Secondary or schematic openings will not lead you to complex positions. You must start to build up a professional repertoire. By this I mean that you must know how to play main openings (the most used by the world's top players nowadays) with both White and Black.
At least you should be able to play at a high level with White either 1.e4 or 1.d4 (Queen's Gambit). And with Black you should be able to respond to 1.e4 with 1.e5 or 1.c5 (Sicilian). Against 1.d4 there are several options such as King's Indian, Grunfeld, Slav, Nimzo-India + derivatives and certain variations of the Queen's Gambit.
Nowadays it is true that with the engines many openings that had a bad reputation become playable again, but there are still first level openings (played by the elite in classical games) and second level openings (playable, but with more difficulties to equalize, sometimes used by the top players as a rapid repertoire).
You should always have at least 1 first level opening and several second level opening

title: Study and the implementation of the new opening repertoire
text:
Unlike tactics and understanding endgames which are easier to understand on your own, it is highly recommended to work on openings and middlegame with a Coach, as you need to be guided and have clear recommendations.
A natural process to incorporate a new opening to your repertoire would be the theoretical study of it focusing on the main lines (lines with more games in the database) since statistically we will have more chances to play them in our games compared to secondary lines.
The time invested in the main lines should be proportional to the number of games played with respect to the total.
If there are 6 variations in a position in the opening, but 90% of the games correspond to only 1 variant, we will invest approximately 90% of our study time in it, logically.
A common mistake is to invest more time than normal in secondary lines that are never played.
Once we have studied the opening, analyzed the typical middlegames and understand well the main ideas, we would go on to put it into online practice to later play it over the board.
My recommendation is to study it thoroughly and practice in 3+2 games. This rhythm will allow us to play a large number of games, lines that we had missed will appear and it will also help us to know which variations are more popular at our level.
Once we have played a significant number of games, we analyze our games, complete our notes on the opening and focus on the typical middlegame plans, recognizing when we play badly and when correctly.
Finally, we repeat this process one or two more times to improve our statistics and gain more confidence before testing our new opening in person.
With practice we will also be able to develop a greater depth and expand our theoretical knowledge by also adapting to the lines that are most repeated.
Once we feel prepared, we test it in class in classical games and as always, we analyze the games afterwards to review the mistakes and possible improvements.
A very important and common mistake that we detected in several of our students was the lack of immediate practice of an opening that we had just taught.
This caused them to forget the theory and despite having the notes they did not understand well the typical plans and concepts of the position.
For this reason, it is essential that Coaches, when explaining openings, do it in the most immediate way possible, avoiding mixing it with classes on other subjects and extending it indefinitely. The student should also commit to practicing the opening as soon as possible after it has been fully explained.
These two points are key to facilitating the student’s learning of openings.
Game analysis in chess is the process of reviewing and examining our played chess games, with the objective of identifying strengths and weaknesses and learning from the mistakes made in order not to repeat them in future games.
summary: Unlike tactics and understanding endgames which are easier to understand on your own, it is highly recommended to work on openings and middlegame with a Coach, as you need to be guided and have clear recommendations. title: Why analyze your chess games
text:
The analysis of games allows us to:
Identify our mistakes: By reviewing a played game, we can identify mistakes and omissions that we have made. In this way, we can take steps to correct these mistakes in the future.
Learn new strategies: Analyzing games will help us identify new ideas and strategies that we might not have considered before.
By comparing our opening with what other players have played we can learn how the pieces develop and the typical plans for that position.
Improve accuracy: We will improve our ability to evaluate positions and make accurate moves. It will help us make better decisions in future games.
Develop the ability to calculate and foresee: It will help us to develop the ability to calculate, foresee and anticipate the moves of our opponents. By studying different variations, we can improve our ability to calculate the possible consequences of our moves.
For all these benefits, game analysis is very beneficial and highly recommended by many coaches.
summary: The analysis of games allows us to: Identify our mistakes: By reviewing a played game, we can identify mistakes and omissions that we have made. In this way, we can take steps to correct these mistakes in the future.

title: At what level to analyze your chess games
text:
Game analysis is very important; however, I notice many coaches using it excessively in their classes regardless of the level of the student and I think it is not always the best approach.
I am going to make a bold statement and surely against the current of many academic philosophies since few chess players and Coaches will deny the usefulness of game analysis, but in my experience, game analysis is useful from an intermediate and high level on, being more and more important as we increase the level. And this has an explanation.
At a beginner, amateur level, where you are just starting to play chess, the number of mistakes that occur in a game is very high and their severity as well.
This is normal since we are starting in a new sport and we still have to learn a lot of basic concepts.
The analysis of games is useful to detect the mistakes and work on them, but at this level there are so many that we cannot focus on a specific topic in particular.
We must work on the basic concepts (chapter 4) to obtain the fundamentals that every chess player should have.
That is why, although game analysis will always add up, it will be much better to spend that training time on learning basic concepts (to the detriment of game analysis) as it will allow us to progress faster.
Only when we have learned these concepts and have progressed adequately will game analysis help us know in which area, we have more problems in our games (openings, middlegame, endgames...) and thus channel and reinforce our training towards those issues.
To draw a parallel, we cannot try to improve our running technique if we do not yet know how to walk.
Game analysis is the process of identifying and perfecting our mistakes. At an amateur level, we already have a long list of essential concepts that must be trained. It is only at more advanced levels when our learning may have been uneven and we need to identify which areas to strengthen.

title: How to analyze your games
text:
At an intermediate or high-level game analysis is necessary and will help you to progress. But how should we do it to get the most out of it?
Game analysis has 2 main functions:
1) To know in which specific area you are making the most mistakes lately and thus channel your training by reinforcing it with related concepts.
2) To analyze specifically the most serious mistakes of each game to understand why we have lost advantage in certain moments of the game.
Game analysis is especially important in games that we have lost. And although we may have made mistakes in games we have won, generally the defeats are the ones that will make us grow, improve and become stronger.
We tend to win against weaker opponents and lose against stronger opponents. If what we are looking for is to grow and progress chess-wise, defeats are more interesting. Invest more time in analyzing games you have lost.
The objective is to not make the same mistakes again so that in case of playing again against the same opponent or a similar rating there is less chance of failure and we can reverse the result.
When analyzing a game, consider all the variables (psychological, time available when making the mistakes, the move in which the mistake was made...) and try to identify what the real mistake was.
Once the mistake is identified, find out what the best way to play in that position would have been and draw a study plan to strengthen that area.
For example, if the problem was time management because you rushed too fast, develop a strategy so that it does not happen again or if you got confused in the opening, make a plan to study it and understand it better.
Ask yourself if it is an isolated mistake or if it is repeated in several of your games.
summary: At an intermediate or high-level game analysis is necessary and will help you to progress. But how should we do it to get the most out of it?

title: Software as a complement to analysis
text:
Nowadays there are many websites and software that are able to identify, according to the evaluation of an engine, where the mistake is.
Currently there are free and very powerful open-Source engines. They are also available on the main chess platforms.
They will show you which moves lose advantage, the most serious mistakes and which the best options in each situation were. This solves one of the parts, that is, we will be able to know where we have failed and what we should have done.
However, we will continue to make the same mistakes if we do not recognize exactly what the general problem is and redirect our training to solve it.
Many chess players think that the engine replaces a Coach and this is far from the truth. Engines are a very useful and helpful tool, but they still do not provide the overview of a coach.
They also have the technical problem of having to know how to interpret them because they handle variables of depth and misuse or misinterpretation can provide false solutions or misdiagnoses.
Take advantage of the engine, analyze what happened, where your mistakes are and design a plan (your own or with your coach) to avoid repeating them.
This is where many players fail and continue to make the same mistakes. Persevere and optimize your games.
summary: Nowadays there are many websites and software that are able to identify, according to the evaluation of an engine, where the mistake is. Currently there are free and very powerful open-Source engines.

title: Depth in game analysis
text:
It is not the same to analyze the chess game just played by a beginner as that of a high-level player. In both cases we will pay attention to different details.
A beginner player is going to make a large number of mistakes. Pointing out all the mistakes may not make much sense as they may be too advanced to understand. The correct thing to do is to explain to that player the most serious mistakes according to their level.
If they have not seen a winning combination of 3 moves, it will be very useful to work on it because they will use their own games to acquire concepts according to their level, while learning a particular theoretical order will not help them to solve the most serious mistakes they are currently making and that are making them lose their games.
As we progress, the most serious mistakes disappear and we should pay attention to mistakes that we did not notice before, such as poor time management or inaccurate opening order.
In short, it is essential to analyze your own games according to the level at which you are in order to continue progressing without difficulties.
Time pressure in chess refer to the situation in which we have already used a large part of the time to think about our moves and it is too short to complete the remaining moves.
In chess competitions, clocks are used to keep track of each player's time and a fixed amount of time is available to finish the game.
Generally, nowadays games are played with increment, i.e., a certain number of seconds is added to each move. A very common international rhythm is 90min + 30s/move.
If a player runs out of time before making their move or finishing the game, they lose on time.
When we practically run out of time, we are said to be in "time trouble".
In this case, it is often necessary to make quick and not necessarily precise moves to avoid defeat by "flag", this means losing by having exhausted the time available for thinking.
Time pressure generate an additional layer of stress and excitement to the games and are an important factor that we have to control in competitions.
summary: It is not the same to analyze the chess game just played by a beginner as that of a high-level player. In both cases we will pay attention to different details.

title: Poor time management in children. Moving too fast
text:
Time management is not easy and depending on the age and level it is very common to always see the same mistakes.
At very early ages, many children play very fast, practically without thinking. They practically ignore the time they have and move instantaneously.
This is a major mistake because we are allowing the opponent to think longer than we do.
Sometimes it will not be enough to defeat us, but at similar levels, those extra minutes can unbalance the scales to determine whether a combination works or not and tip the game to one side or the other.
This is normal because children generally have not yet developed patience.
It is very important that they gradually get used to playing longer games and thinking more. How do we solve this?
One of the techniques we advise to progressively get children to think more is simply to make the child commit to at least a certain number of minutes per game in the chair (for example 30 minutes), even if they do not use them to think, they can even look around during their turn.
Once the child is able to sit for 30 minutes, does not get nervous, has no need to stand up, they will start to invest those minutes in thinking. Gradually, they will be thinking longer without realizing it until they manage it properly.
This technique is another strategy that was applied with me when I started and it helped me a lot to progress.
Gradually I understood that the more I thought the better moves I made and the better results I got.
summary: Time management is not easy and depending on the age and level it is very common to always see the same mistakes. At very early ages, many children play very fast, practically without thinking.

title: Poor time management in children. Moving too slowly
text:
Interestingly at the Academy, although with far fewer cases we have also noticed the reverse behavior, i.e., time-consuming children who find it difficult to decide on a move.
A priori we might think that they are developing reflection and it is something positive and in part it is so, but it is also a problem when it comes to being competitive.
In case of time trouble, they must react quickly and as they lack that tension because they have not practiced it, they usually make serious mistakes.
Generally, these students prefer to play long games where they can think practically without worrying about time.
A very effective solution is to suggest that they play Blitz 3+2 games to favor decision making.
We have tested it and it helps them to calculate faster, gain confidence and make instant decisions if necessary.
