title: Current time pressure at intermediate and high levels
text:
One of the keys that Carlsen has gotten the most out of in recent years is time management and this has allowed him to always be at a higher level. He places a lot of importance on it and it is vital today.
Carlsen is known for defeating world tops in seemingly evenly rated positions but where you have to play precise.
The reason is that he has a great theoretical knowledge in openings which allows him to play the first moves fast and get a big time advantage over his opponents.
When the time comes, the opponent has many more options to make mistakes.
Nowadays, with the boom of material and information about chess and the optimization of the engines, it is easier to progress quickly in chess.
In recent years, FIDE has been shortening the time to think in classical games (in the past they used to play games of 6 hours plus adjournments). The reason is to induce players to arrive earlier to the time pressure to force more mistakes, generate imbalances and reduce the number of draws.
I have come to the conclusion that nowadays, in order to be competitive, you cannot be in time trouble or at least if you do you must always have more time than your opponent.
Nobody decides to be short of time, that's for sure. So how do we optimize our time management?
To be our best competitive version at a high level nowadays, we must play the opening faster than our opponent.
This is key and the process demands quite a few hours to be able to do it well and safely. It consists of two parts:
-First, we must have our professional opening repertoire (Chapter 6). A repertoire that is not just the meaningless memorization of the first moves, but that includes the typical middlegame plans.
Having a good opening repertoire will help us to be able to play the first moves without consuming time and to start investing time seriously from at least move 10-15.
A common mistake is to think that if a chess game consists of three phases (opening, middlegame and endgame), one third of the time should be spent on the opening. At a high level, this is never the case.
The openings are pre-worked in training and what it allows is a very big saving in time. We make sure that we play the right plans and we’ll know the middlegames.
Again, we stress the importance of not studying openings at a low-intermediate level, always prioritizing the consolidation of a good solid base of concepts.
This phase of optimization in openings is part of the improvement of a chess player that we assume is well nourished with elementary concepts and ideas (as a reference: 1800 rating).
-The second key to playing the opening fast is to avoid preparations and this implies a repertoire of several openings.
If the opponent is able to prepare quickly against your openings because you always play the same, even if they have less theoretical knowledge, they will play you as fast as you do or faster. Nowadays all players prepare their games beforehand.

summary: One of the keys that Carlsen has gotten the most out of in recent years is time management and this has allowed him to always be at a higher level. He places a lot of importance on it and it is vital today.

title: Masters also make mistakes in time pressure
text:
There are times when analyzing games that the student thinks that they have made a serious tactical mistake and that is why they have lost the game, and this may be partially true. But when we are in time pressure, poor time management can be the main culprit.
We explain this to our students. Even Grandmasters and elite players make very serious mistakes (sometimes beginner's mistakes) when they are pressed for time. How can we not make them?
The key is to try not to get into time trouble. When we want to be competitive, we have to value time as another factor of the position.
Positions with a winning valuation but difficult to play can even be easily lost if time is not available.
Nobody wants to get into time trouble, but are you playing the opening quickly so that you can spend more time on middlegame and endgame (the most complex parts of a game)?
Do you try to have at least more time than your opponent? Do you adapt your tempo to a faster one in case you fall behind your opponent's time?
summary: There are times when analyzing games that the student thinks that they have made a serious tactical mistake and that is why they have lost the game, and this may be partially true. But when we are in time pressure, poor time management can be the main culprit.

title: Never think more than 20 minutes on a move
text:
If you spend more than 20 minutes thinking about a single move, the move you make will probably be a bad one. Has this ever happened to you?
It is a very common mistake. We have calculated so many variations, discarded so many options that our mind is lost and we end up playing a meaningless random move that is usually a very bad one.
Although it may seem illogical, this occurs quite often. Thinking more does not imply that you are going to find the best move. An excess of time thinking about a single move makes the mind get confused and saturated and we end up opting for inferior lines.
summary: If you spend more than 20 minutes thinking about a single move, the move you make will probably be a bad one. Has this ever happened to you?

title: If your opponent has more time than you, make up for it. You must play faster
text:
You don't always get out of the opening well. Lines are forgotten, we are surprised, an unexpected preparation...
And in some games, we are worse in the opening and therefore we must invest time to not end up lost.
Our opponent has more time, but we had no choice.
This case should be something unusual, but sometimes it happens.
The opponent now has a lot of time for both middlegame and endgame. If you survive from the opening, but reach the middlegame or endgame with practically no time, you will end up losing because these are the most complex phases of a game. Remember?
Make up those minutes little by little until you have the same amount of time available to think as your opponent does.
When the danger phase of the opening passes and your opponent starts to think, it will also be vital to take some risks and play fast to avoid problems also in the middlegame and endgame.
This is the only way to be able to equalize the game completely.
If you choose to think and always be behind in the clock, in many occasions it ends in a slow death. The moment you reach the time pressure with a complex position you will end up making a mistake.
And this mistake will not be tactical or of calculation, although many will attribute it to that, but of time management.
summary: You don't always get out of the opening well. Lines are forgotten, we are surprised, an unexpected preparation...

title: Ways to practice Time Management
text:
In general, the most suitable rhythm for practicing time management could be 3+2 or 5+3, where the predicaments are going to appear early and we should try to play the opening fast.
If the time pressure at an intermediate-high level is due to lack of confidence in some cases even the practice of Bullet 2+1 or 1+1 could be recommended as a specific exercise to free the mind, avoid blockages and work more on our intuition.
Generally, we advise against the practice of Bullet because, although it can improve these aspects in the long run, it generates habits that are not advisable for classical games.
However, there is no problem in practicing it in a timely and constructive manner.
These topics are very interesting and affect especially at an advanced level, since they are part of refinement, but every chess player can apply them to get the best version of themselves.

title: How to feed yourself to compete properly before a chess game
text:
In my last norms to get the title of International Master I happened to be working with a nutritionist, not so much to achieve some goals in the competition as to learn how to eat healthily.
I must admit that I learned a lot and it helped me to apply certain techniques and achieve better results when I compete.
Of course, it is a very broad field and each chess player prioritizes or approaches it in different ways. I found these tips very useful.
I played at my best level and I would like to share them with you.
The best meals are those that release energy slowly and allow you to play long games in a stable way without having performance drops.
These foods are: all kinds of vegetables, legumes or carbohydrates such as salads, beans, cabbage, pasta, rice...
Vegetables are characterized by being an important source of essential nutrients, including vitamins, minerals and fiber.
These nutrients help keep the body healthy and functioning properly during the game.
In addition, they are rich in antioxidants that can help reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, which is beneficial for brain function.
Legumes are an excellent source of protein, fiber and complex carbohydrates, making them an ideal food for any athlete, including chess players.
The complex carbohydrates present in legumes are digested slowly and provide sustained energy for the brain and body that is very beneficial in long chess games.
In addition, they are also rich in iron, an essential mineral for the body that helps transport oxygen to the tissues and muscles, important to be well during the game.
Carbohydrates are an important source of energy for the body.
When carbohydrates are consumed, the body converts them into glucose, which is used as a source of energy for the brain and muscles.
All of them are beneficial for concentration and endurance during a game of chess and competition.
There are also some foods that you should avoid. Mainly you should avoid heavy meals that cause the body's blood during the game to be in the stomach instead of the brain.
If you eat heavy food, you will also get drowsy and you will not be 100% concentrated.
Some foods that you should not eat before a game are:
-Fried food: It is rich in saturated fats and can be difficult to digest. In addition, fried food can increase the risk of digestive discomfort.
-Red meat: Red meat is also rich in saturated fats and can be difficult to digest. In addition, it takes a lot of energy and time to digest, which can make you feel drowsy during the game.
-Spicy food: Spicy food can cause heartburn, which can affect your ability to concentrate during the game.
And under no circumstances should you eat food with high sugar content.
Foods with high sugar content, such as candy, sweets, candy bars, chocolate bars, soft drinks or coffee may provide an initial burst of energy, but can then cause a drop in blood sugar levels, which can lead to fatigue and drowsiness.

title: Be physically active
text:
In the old days, people smoked while playing chess, consumed large amounts of coffee, and physical sport made little difference.
Chess has changed, it has become more professional and more and more, all the little details count.
Nowadays all elite chess players exercise and train physically. Anand admitted in an interview that he trained at least 2 hours a day in the gym.
The reason is obvious. Generally, chess games last 4 hours or even more and involve a brutal energy drain.
To be able to play the decisive parts of the game properly you must be fit and get there with maximum energy.
Karpov lost 10 kilos in 1984 defending the title of World Chess Champion against Kasparov. In chess a lot of tension builds up and a lot of energy is needed.
The practice of sport will also help you to reduce stress, improve concentration and improve cardiovascular and respiratory function which will increase the flow of oxygen and nutrients to the brain.
In short, you will have more energy to compete better.
summary: In the old days, people smoked while playing chess, consumed large amounts of coffee, and physical sport made little difference. Chess has changed, it has become more professional and more and more, all the little details count.

title: Rest in competition
text:
Like food and sport, rest is related to the energy we have to compete.
Rest is an important component of competing well in chess because it affects the ability to concentrate, mental performance and our decision making.
Chess is a mental sport, but it can also be physically exhausting. The body needs rest and recovery after long games, especially if you have been sitting for hours.
If not, enough rest time is allowed, muscles can become strained, which can affect our comfort and concentration.
Mental fatigue can reduce the ability to concentrate, which can affect decision making and the ability to think clearly.
A good rest can help improve mood and mental capacity to fight more in games. It also helps relieve mental stress and improve performance.
Rest is also important to prepare for upcoming games.
If we accumulate fatigue we will compete at a lower performance as the tournament progresses.
Rest is one of the most critical and underrated elements. It is considered that children should sleep at least 8 to 9 hours and adults 7 to 8 hours. Excessive rest time would also be counterproductive.
summary: Like food and sport, rest is related to the energy we have to compete. Rest is an important component of competing well in chess because it affects the ability to concentrate, mental performance and our decision making.

title: Circadian rhythm. Lark, intermediate or owl?
text:
Humans have a natural circadian rhythm, which refers to the roughly 24-hour cycle that regulates biological processes in our bodies, such as sleep, body temperature, and hormone release. Exposure to light and darkness is one of the main factors regulating the circadian rhythm.
People who have a natural tendency to sleep later and wake up later are called “owls”, which is known as the evening chronotype. I am one of them and curiously many of the chess players are too. This is why many of the big players only play 1 round tournaments in the afternoon.
This means that our circadian rhythm shifts to later and therefore we often have a hard time waking up early in the morning and feel sleepy during the early hours of the day. This can be problematic if we have rounds in the morning.
On the other hand, people who have a natural tendency to wake up early and go to bed early are called "larks", which is known as the morning chronotype. This means that their circadian rhythm shifts to earlier, and therefore they tend to feel more alert and productive in the early hours of the day.
People with an intermediate chronotype have a circadian rhythm that is somewhere in the middle between the morning and evening chronotype.
They can often adjust to both morning and evening rounds, but may have trouble maintaining a regular sleep schedule.
Statistically, the most common chronotype is intermediate (approximately 50% and the other half is divided between owls and larks).
It is also very useful to know which group we belong to in order to be more productive when studying and learning chess. Specifically, I have greater concentration, I am calmer and I am more productive at night. And you? Find out when you are most productive and take advantage of it to learn in those hours and compete in those moments of the day.
summary: Humans have a natural circadian rhythm, which refers to the roughly 24-hour cycle that regulates biological processes in our bodies, such as sleep, body temperature, and hormone release. Exposure to light and darkness is one of the main factors regulating the circadian rhythm.

title: Walk during the game to reduce mental fatigue and stress
text:
There are chess players who like to sit for the entire game and others who get up practically every move. The optimum is probably somewhere in between, although every chess player is different.
It is advisable to take regular breaks if sitting for long periods of time, as is common in many office activities.
The same is true in chess.
It is recommended to take frequent short breaks of at least 5 to 10 minutes every hour to stretch your legs, walk around a bit and rest your eyes.
This is because sitting for long periods of time can have negative effects such as back, neck and shoulder pain, poor blood circulation and fatigue.
Walking on the opponent's turn will help reduce tension in the body and improve blood circulation, which can help prevent these negative effects.
In addition, it will also improve our concentration as it helps reduce mental fatigue and stress. That is why many chess players stand up after playing their move.
Although you may think that by sitting all the time you will be more concentrated, you may get a better performance if you walk around and take a break from time to time.
summary: There are chess players who like to sit for the entire game and others who get up practically every move. The optimum is probably somewhere in between, although every chess player is different.

title: Plan travel and accommodations strategically. Take care of yourself at an older age or higher level
text:
Organize and plan your tournament, how you are going to go, where you are going to stay, where you are going to play...
It is common to see chess players who travel to a tournament who start their first round badly because they make very long trips on the same day or have to drive for long hours. They arrive to compete tired on the first day.
Also, do not stay far from the competition venue as long journeys before the game can cause you to be worn out or dizzy and not at your best.
You should always take care of yourself, but especially more so at an older age and at a higher level.
Every chess player can improve using these techniques.
However, there are two key factors that will make this section even more important for better performance.
1) Age. The younger you are, the more vitality you possess and therefore more energy. I would distinguish 3 periods.
Up to the age of 18, the body has plenty of energy to compete at a high level without worrying too much about these issues. Everything that is done would help to optimize our results.
From 18 to 40 years, we enter the maturity phase, the body suffers more and directly affects performance.
From the age of 40 onwards, the body and mind begin to decline and neglecting one of these three pillars can lead to a significant drop in performance.
2) Level. While at a low level many of the games are decided tactically and by pure strategic knowledge of chess... at an intermediate-high level many of the games are decided on the details.
The higher the level, the more important it is to eat well, to be well rested and to be in good physical shape.
Learning chess is key, as is competing and preparing for tournaments properly. In this chapter we are going to analyze the most important factors and the most common questions I usually receive.
summary: Organize and plan your tournament, how you are going to go, where you are going to stay, where you are going to play... It is common to see chess players who travel to a tournament who start their first round badly because they make very long trips on the same day or have to drive for long hours.

title: Choice of tournaments according to age and level
text:
The ideal to progress in chess is to compete against stronger opponents than you. The ideal profile is those players who have a slightly higher rating or ranking.
You will play balanced games, there will be no big disadvantages and you will not win or lose easily.
The main reason is that after playing the game you will have very interesting material to analyze later, in addition to the fact that the drawn games are usually decided in endgames, they are extended in time and will make you try harder and think more.
A game that has been won easily will not provide you with much didactic content. If you have lost you will learn more, but if the difference is very large it is possible that the game be over too soon, it can be frustrating and you will not deal with concepts appropriate to your level.
The second reason, although it is more secondary, is that you will have serious chances to score if you are training well and your rating will improve quickly, which can motivate you more to keep training hard. It is more important to learn than to focus on improving our rating.
For children who are just starting out, it is highly recommended to play against other children of the same age because it will help them to socialize, make friends and use chess as a common link.
The difference of one year at early ages can mean a big change of level since it represents a very high percentage of their whole life and therefore there are usually differences in knowledge between older and younger children.
If children excel in chess, have interest and want to continue improving quickly, it is very important that they start playing against adults, that is to say, open tournaments (not limited by age).
Adults make different mistakes and it will help them to be more patient, think more and gain experience. They also have a more stable ranking while children are in a learning phase and usually have an underrated score.
At intermediate and high-level open tournaments are also the most interesting. In some countries you can choose which section of the tournament to play in.
Again, if possible, a section higher than ours would be ideal to play against stronger opponents and allow us to learn more.
At a very high level, especially when you want to achieve International Master or Grandmaster norms (performances in tournaments with specific FIDE requirements), you can also play closed tournaments.
In closed tournaments it is ensured that all participants are eligible to achieve these standards. Mainly to be able to play with the required number of foreign players and a specific rating average.
In an open tournament it may be the case that after achieving a very good performance you cannot access a norm because you have had the misfortune to play with players of the same nationality or with several players with a very low rating and have greatly affected the average rating of your opponents.
summary: The ideal to progress in chess is to compete against stronger opponents than you. The ideal profile is those players who have a slightly higher rating or ranking.

title: Choice of tournaments according to the time control
text:
We can classify tournaments into one-day tournaments (Blitz or rapid) and multi-day tournaments (classical pace). Both are allowed by FIDE and their function is different.
The most important tournaments that really show the progress of a player are the classical tournaments.
All our training should be focused on improving in this type of tournaments.
The rapid tournaments are often used as a form of leisure because they are entertaining.
It can also be a good way to get back in touch with the board after a long time of inactivity or to try new openings recently studied.
It is also common to see unusual gambits or even dubious lines played taking advantage of the fact that the opponent does not have much time to solve them at the board.
If your objective is exclusively entertainment and you play in these tournaments only occasionally, it does not have much importance, but keep in mind that you are missing an opportunity to practice some new opening, it can generate bad habits and you may end up transferring them to more classical rhythms.
Some chess players even have a specific repertoire for rapid. Except for the top 100 in the world, it doesn't make much sense to invest time in it. Even if you don't compete regularly in rapid tournaments, it's fine.
Prepare well for classical tournaments and try to be active during the year. If you play occasionally, you will find it hard to get your mind ready to think about long games.
summary: We can classify tournaments into one-day tournaments (Blitz or rapid) and multi-day tournaments (classical pace). Both are allowed by FIDE and their function is different.

title: Choice of tournaments according to their format
text:
Classic tournaments are mainly divided into double-round tournaments (two rounds per day, usually morning and afternoon) and single-round tournaments (one round per day).
What does this mean for a chess player? The double-round tournament requires more daily energy and therefore less time to rest.
This mainly favors young chess players with a lot of vitality, physically fit.
Double round tournaments are especially ideal for children and young people.
Having to play morning and afternoon, in case of having had a long game in the morning can cause a strong drop in performance and usually influences more adults and senior or veteran chess players.
Tournaments of one round a day are highly recommended for adults as it allows them to rest enough to recover and to be able to rethink each game with energy.
A recommended option for veterans to compete at their highest level is to request strategic breaks in 1 or 2 rounds thus reducing the number of games, resting on those days and allowing better performances.
Team competitions that in many countries are played one round every Saturday or Sunday can also be a good alternative for them and get them to play again at their full performance.

title: Game preparation
text:
Game preparation would be the process by which players analyze the opponent and study the openings, their statistics and ways of playing that may arise during the game.
Game preparation is carried out in order to play the opening quickly and well, to have more time on the clock and to maximize the chances of winning the game.
This is achieved through careful analysis of the opponent's previous games, identification of their strengths and weaknesses and proper selection of the opening that can do the most damage to our opponent.
The preparation of games is an important part nowadays when competing at intermediate and high level, as professional players usually devote many hours to this preparation.
For this reason, we mentioned the importance of having a flexible repertoire that allows us to play several openings and be unpredictable.

title: Types of game preparations
text:
We could classify game preparations into two types:
1)  Specific preparation against our opponent (attacking their weaknesses):
If we know that our opponent always plays the same way against a particular order, we can study what the engines suggest and what the world tops have played in those positions, even if it is not our usual opening.
The more times our opponent repeats the same lines, the more chances we have that they play our preparation in the game.
In this case there is a risk that our opponent changes their usual way of playing to avoid our preparation and we have to play an opening with which we are not familiar.
To avoid this, we should analyze the statistics and games available in the database to have a greater certainty that we will play the lines studied.
It can also be that they have studied our games and suspect a preparation if we play a line that we do not usually play. There is a risk that they improvise and do not play our preparation.
2)  Optimizing our repertoire (strengthening our weaknesses):
Generally, at an intermediate or high level it will be difficult to know exactly what lines we are going to play. We will not be able to go deep because it is common for our opponents to play several variations.
Therefore, a very interesting option is to review and expand our knowledge on the opening that we already use and we are sure of, or that we have high chances of playing.
How does it differ from the previous preparation? In several ways. The main one is that you review a usual line or opening that you already play normally to strengthen yourself, it is not a new specific line taking advantage of the opponent's weakness.
The advantage of this is that the time you invest will always be useful and you will be able to use it even in other games, while if you prepare a new line, it will only be useful for a single game and a specific opponent.
You also review a larger number of lines, but in a more general way. Since we do not know exactly what we are going to play, we must be sure to review main and secondary lines and not in much depth. As we advance in moves it is more unlikely that our preparation will coincide with what we are going to play.
Which method is better? It really depends on the situation and statistics also play a role. If we have an opponent who always does the same thing, preparing against them will give us good chances to achieve a good middlegame and even win the game without thinking if we locate a great weakness in their repertoire.
If, on the other hand, it is more difficult to deduce what they are going to play or they are an opponent with a wide repertoire, preparing to reinforce and expand our knowledge will be more useful in the long run.

title: The best preparation is to have a good training in our daily routine
text:
Study work should not be done during the tournament.
A common mistake is to prepare very intensively for a game (some chess players dedicate up to 3 or 4 hours of preparation) and then lack the energy to be able to play.
If we study a lot of chess before playing our game, our energy will drop a lot and we will not play at our maximum performance. In the end it is about making the best moves, not about analyzing the opponent more and for that we must be relaxed, rested and have energy.
Also, in many cases it is not easy to predict what we are going to play and we will hardly win with preparation alone. Study hard while training and in tournaments dedicate yourself and focus on applying the acquired concepts. Ian Nepomniachtchi (World Champion Candidate) shared this same reflection in an interview.
summary: Study work should not be done during the tournament. A common mistake is to prepare very intensively for a game (some chess players dedicate up to 3 or 4 hours of preparation) and then lack the energy to be able to play.

title: Preparation of games for important Cadet Championships (World Championships, Pan-American...)
text:
The concepts explained above are useful for all types of championships, including those with the highest demands.
It will always be important to rest, to have trained previously and to play without pressure.
I have worked as a coach for the U-8, U-10 and U-12 U.S. National Team, as well as preparing some of my students for the World and Pan American Championships, some of which they even won. And yes, there are some nuances that it would be good to point out.
In the most demanding International Championships, the preparation of games is more decisive the younger the age of the category.
The reason is that many children have hardly had time to build up a repertoire and tend to play always the same, which makes them predictable, especially in U-8 and U-10 categories.
In many cases we have prepared games to achieve winning positions where the opponent practically had to abandon. Generally, these are type 1 preparations (specific against our opponent).
At this age children make many serious mistakes and repeat their openings frequently. If we track them down, we have a good chance of getting a winning position.
As age increases, children become more flexible and it is more difficult to predict the specific openings or lines they will play. They also tend to choose to try new lines before repeating variations they have played previously and they play better, they do not make serious mistakes that can be easily attacked.
At ages U-14 and above, we usually use a type 2 preparation (optimizing our repertoire) because it is already difficult to predict their mistakes.
Even so, it can be a great advantage because, if we know the typical plans, we can play quickly and have an advantage in the clock facing the middlegame much better.
But remember that preparation will not save you if you have not trained properly the previous months.
summary: The concepts explained above are useful for all types of championships, including those with the highest demands. It will always be important to rest, to have trained previously and to play without pressure.

title: How to avoid preparations
text:
We have already seen that preparations can be an extra support to the chess player's knowledge, so it is very important to avoid any kind of preparation or at least minimize its risk.
Two factors play a role. The games of yours that your opponent has at their disposal and the number of openings you know or the flexibility you have in playing different lines.
Nowadays, many of the games are broadcast or tournament organizers collect them and at that moment they become part of various existing online and offline databases.
Just play tournaments of a certain level and your games will appear, making it easier for your opponents to prepare. This cannot be avoided, you cannot stop playing tournaments, but you can know what lines you have played and what information your opponents have about you.
If while playing a game, your opponent is repeating the same moves from another game in which you were inferior, consider the option of including an improvement or deviating from the line you played or you will end up in just as bad a position again. Another important point that has recently been taken into account is online games. If you have a public profile, it is possible that your opponents can access it and see what you have been practicing lately.
Of course, the repertoire played in an international classical tournament does not have the same value as that played in online Blitz games, however, it can be a great sample for your rivals and you will surely have generated a large number of games.
The solution is very simple. Practice your repertoire that you will apply in tournaments with anonymous accounts that do not identify you. You can use a public account to play online with unusual openings or simply for entertainment.
As a curiosity, during the preparation of a World Championship we got great material through games played on online platforms, even getting to know the preparation that the opponent did and was going to put into practice that day. Protect your privacy!
And the second factor is flexibility. In this case, there are several options. Ideally, you should be able to play several openings well.
The main drawback is that it requires a lot of time and the ideal is to study it at an advanced level.
An intermediate option is at least to have several lines of the same opening, so that the opponent does not know 100% which variant you are going to use and does not have so much time to delve into the opening.
In the worst-case scenario, if we are surprised with a preparation, we should try to get out as soon as possible and look for positions that are playable and break out of the main lines that our opponent has prepared.
We will always have the option of using the basic concepts by playing a new position and applying the general classical ideas of chess that we have learned with our experience.
And in all cases, keep calm, do not get nervous and evaluate which solution can be the best to counteract that initial preparation.
summary: We have already seen that preparations can be an extra support to the chess player's knowledge, so it is very important to avoid any kind of preparation or at least minimize its risk. Two factors play a role.
